title: Well-timed emergency credit can reduce post-disaster financial collapse
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 32845; Federal Disaster Loan applications linked to pre- and post-shock credit records
geography: United States households with uninsured damage from federally declared natural disasters and Federal Disaster Loan applications

observations.period: U.S. disaster-loan applicants and post-disaster outcomes; paper issued 2024

denominator.unit: Federal Disaster Loan applicant panel with uninsured disaster damage

identification.value: loan approval rules made applicants below a 40% debt-to-income ratio differentially likely to be approved; the study uses an instrumented difference-in-differences design

bankruptcy.value: credit provision reduced the likelihood of filing for bankruptcy by 61% in the three years following the disaster

mechanism.value: additional quasi-experimental variation in interest rates supports a liquidity-based explanation

car_purchases.value: credit provision increased car purchases even three years after loan receipt

observations.method: The authors link Federal Disaster Loan application data to a panel of credit records before and after a negative shock, exploit the loan-approval debt-to-income discontinuity, and estimate an instrumented difference-in-differences effect with additional quasi-experimental interest-rate variation.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not observe the household's exact damaged asset, repair, insurance payment, other aid, family support, work, health, care, housing, or consumption path. It does not compare loans with grants or direct repair, measure repayment burden and missed essentials, or establish outcomes for people unable to apply or outside the Federal Disaster Loan population.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households applying for Federal Disaster Loans after uninsured damage from federally declared natural disasters; approval effects may differ by debt-to-income ratio, disaster, asset, credit access, and household resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower bankruptcy and additional car purchases show meaningful financial protection in this setting but do not prove that every loan improved welfare or that debt was harmless. A car purchase may preserve work and care access or add a repayment burden; the study does not identify the complete household use of funds.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 32845

boundary: This record adds a causal emergency-liquidity finding: well-timed disaster credit reduced bankruptcy and increased later car purchases among the studied applicants. It does not establish full recovery, repayment safety, health or job continuity, equal access, or the superiority of loans over grants or other aid.
